newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian maize production growing by 5.3 pct/yr.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian maize production growing by 5.3 pct/yr.

text.p: Nigerian maize production has grown by 5.3 percent a year since 1993 compared with 3.5 percent increases between 1982 and 1992, the spokesman for an institute on crops research said on Friday.

"The yearly increase of Nigerias maize production has been phenomenal," Taye Babaleye, spokesman for the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), told Reuters by telephone from its south-western Ibadan base.
"The main reason for this is the introduction by the IITA of high-yielding, drought-tolerant and extra-early maturing varieties of the grain," Babaleye added.
"This variety has a yield potential of five tonnes per hectare of land."
He did not provide comparative figures for the yield potential or give annual tonnage production figures.
He said the IITA expected further increase in Nigerias annual maize production between the next three to four years, as long as natural and human disasters did not occur.
The extra-early maturing maize could be harvested 60 days after cultivation compared to 120 days for conventional maize, he said.
"We had to develop this variety so that farmers in the North where drought is common can harvest maize early enough."
Northern Nigeria has Sahelian weather with only scant rainfall.
Babaleye said there was also the need to meet demand by Nigerian breweries who now use maize in beer production as well as satisfying the increasing demand of a growing population.
Nigeria has a population of 100 million, Africas biggest concentration.
Maize is an essential food for most families in the West African country where it is eaten boiled or roasted.
Babaleye said: "That boiled or roasted green maize is now a common sight along roadsides in the villages and urban centres is evidence of high maize yield in Nigeria."
The early-maturing maize became a research objective at the IITA in 1984, he said, adding "After recording successes in our experiments, we began to cultivate the variety in the early 1990s."
